prompt:
Write an essay of about 1,500 words on whether primary schools should still teach joined-up handwriting. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it with more confidence than many of them currently do, because the case against it rests on a picture of what children need that is narrower than what a child actually does with a pen in the seven years between five and eleven. The case is usually put like this: nobody will write by hand as an adult except for shopping lists and signatures, keyboards are faster, curriculum time is scarce, and the looped, slanted script that grandparents remember is a Victorian accomplishment that survives only because teachers were taught it by teachers who were taught it. Each of those premises contains some truth, and I think the conclusion still fails, for reasons that have to do with how children learn to write, how they think while they write, and what a school is for when it decides how to spend a quarter of an hour on a Tuesday.

Begin with the premise that handwriting is obsolete, because that is where the argument gets its force. It is true that adults type most of what they produce, and it is true that a child who is eleven now will spend working life at a screen. It does not follow that handwriting stops mattering in school, since school is where the child is still being built, and the tools used while building a mind are not the same as the tools the finished adult will pick up. A child in a primary classroom writes by hand for most of the day: spelling tests, number work, science observations, comprehension answers, every exam sat before the age of eleven. Whatever else is said about the future, the present for these children is a pencil, and a child who cannot write fluently with one is working with a handicap that costs her attention in every lesson. Fluency matters because the mechanical act of forming letters competes for the same limited working memory as the thinking that the letters are meant to carry. Virginia Berninger and her colleagues found, in a long series of studies with school-age children, that those with more automatic handwriting wrote longer and better compositions, and that the effect was visible in the quality of the ideas as well as the neatness of the page. A child still labouring over each letter has less attention left for what the sentence is supposed to say, and joined writing, done well, is the quickest route to the point at which the hand stops demanding attention.

I should be honest that the evidence on speed is less tidy than enthusiasts of cursive like to suggest. Studies comparing joined and printed writing have not found that one is reliably faster for every child, and a fluent printer can outpace a hesitant joiner. What the better studies suggest is that the choice of script matters less than whether the child has been taught one properly and practised it until it is automatic. That is an argument for teaching handwriting well, and it points toward joined writing for a practical reason that is easy to overlook: printed letters require the pen to leave the page after every stroke, so that a word is a series of separate events, whereas a joined word is a single movement with a rhythm of its own. A child who writes a word in one continuous motion is also practising the word as a unit, which is a plausible reason why spelling seems to benefit when children learn to join early, since the hand remembers the shape of common letter strings such as the ending of "ing" or "tion" in a way that a sequence of isolated marks does not. Teachers of dyslexic children have long argued along these lines, and although the research here is thinner than anyone would like, the reasoning is sound and the experience of practitioners is consistent.

The deeper reason to teach handwriting, joined or otherwise, has come from neuroscience over the last fifteen years, and it is the part of the debate where the keyboard advocates have the most to answer. Karin James and her team showed that young children who learned letters by drawing them showed more activity in the reading-related regions of the brain afterwards than children who learned the same letters by typing or tracing, and the difference was attributed to the variability of hand-drawn forms, which forces the child to extract what makes an "a" an "a" across many slightly different attempts. A keyboard gives every "a" an identical shape, and the child learns the location of a key instead of the structure of a letter. More recently, a Norwegian team using EEG found widespread connectivity across the brain in students who wrote by hand compared with those who typed, a pattern associated with memory formation and learning. These studies are small, and the researchers themselves are cautious about what follows for classrooms, so nobody should treat them as proof that cursive makes children cleverer. They do establish that the hand and the eye and the language centres of the brain are doing something together during handwriting that they are not doing during typing, and a school that drops the practice should have strong evidence that nothing is lost, which no one has produced.

The usual reply is that this applies to handwriting in general and leaves the question of joining untouched, so that children could simply print and enjoy the cognitive benefits without the extra burden of a second script. That is the strongest form of the opposing case, and it deserves a direct answer. The answer is that the burden is smaller than critics suppose and the benefits of joining are real. Children who learn a printed alphabet at five and are asked to change to a joined one at seven are being taught two systems, which is wasteful, but the remedy is to teach joined forms from the start, as many schools in England and elsewhere now do, with entry and exit strokes built into the letters from the first week. A child taught this way never learns a second alphabet; she learns one alphabet that is designed to be written without lifting the pen. The reversals that trouble young writers, the b and the d, are also easier to avoid when each letter begins on the line with a lead-in stroke and the two shapes begin from different places. Montessori schools and many European systems have taught writing this way for a century, and the children in them do not seem to suffer.

There is also the matter of what happens to children who never become fluent at either, since the argument that print is good enough tends to be made by people who write well. A great many children leave primary school with handwriting that is slow, effortful and barely legible, and for them the consequences are real: examiners find their answers harder to read and mark them accordingly, and the children themselves come to hate writing, which spreads to a dislike of putting thoughts on paper at all. Dropping the formal teaching of joined writing would not remove this problem; it would remove the one part of the curriculum that is designed to address it, and the children who would suffer most are those without a parent at home who sits with them and makes them practise. Middle-class families will go on teaching their children to write properly, because they understand that it matters for exams and for the impression a child gives a teacher, and the gap will widen in the way that gaps in unglamorous skills always widen when schools stop treating them as part of the job.

The time objection is the one with the most practical weight, because the curriculum is crowded and every minute is contested. But handwriting practice is not a block of time that sits beside the rest of the day. A fifteen-minute daily session, which is about what the better programmes recommend, is the cheapest intervention in the primary curriculum, requiring a pencil and a lined page, and the fluency it produces pays back across the rest of the timetable by making every written task a little less costly. If schools are short of time, the place to look is not the one subject that makes all the others easier to complete.

None of this requires nostalgia, and the best defence of joined-up handwriting is not that it is beautiful or traditional, though it can be both. Children should also learn to type, and by the end of primary school they should be able to do so with reasonable speed, since keyboards will be part of their working lives and a school that ignored them would be failing its pupils in a different direction. The two skills are not competitors, any more than reading aloud and reading silently are competitors, and a child who has both is better equipped than a child who has one. What the teaching of joined writing offers, in the end, is a hand that can keep up with a mind, a body of practice that seems to help the brain learn the shapes of language, and a skill that costs little to teach and a great deal to lack. Those are the grounds on which any school subject should be judged, and by them it earns its place in the timetable of every primary school.
